extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers of Popular Science Monthly interested in health, longevity, and mental hygiene
extracted.subtask_short: advice on longevity and mental health
extracted.subtask_description: Popular-science guidance on factors that favor great age and on diagnosing, preventing, and treating mental breakdown caused by 'worry' (as distinct from mere overwork). Includes observational guidance about making claims on climate and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors associated with longevity / centenarian regimen
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of centenarians have made their regimen known. Notwithstanding some rare examples to the contrary, temperance, sobriety, and regularity of habits, are of the first importance; then follow heredity, a relatively comfortable condition, freedom from strong and frequent emotions, residence as far as possible in the country, exercise, and a healthy and quiet business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hoffmann's concise summary: "Avoid excess in everything, respect old habits, even bad ones, breathe a pure air, adapt your food to your temperament, shun medicines and doctors, keep a quiet conscience, a gay heart, a contented mind." (Use of these practices is presented as the practical regimen many centenarians followed.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid narcotizing warning sensations with stimulants/medicines
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of stimulants in aid of work (alcohol, coffee, tea, opium, chloral, etc.) narcotizes the sense of weariness so that the reserve of energy is appropriated and injury may follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake temporary masking of fatigue for added energy; stimulants do not add to the stock of energy but suspend warning senses and permit depletion and 'depreciation' of reserves. Shun medicines and doctors is advised in the longevity section; the worry article similarly warns against stupefying drugs as enabling dangerous overuse of reserves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worry (mental disquietude) as primary cause of mental collapse (not overwork)
rubrics_metrics.description: "When a strong and active mind breaks down suddenly, in the midst of business, it is worn out by worry rather than over-work." Worry is described as disorder produced by mental disquietude and distraction which interrupts the natural rhythm of mental energy and suspends the warning sense guarding reserves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The argument: overwork (in normal, natural mode) is unlikely to exhaust reserves because warning sensations guard them; worry introduces external morbid influences that disable these safeguards and expose reserves to loss and lasting injury. Therefore prevention/treatment should target worry rather than merely reducing work volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symptoms/indicators of worry-induced breakdown
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs that worry has impaired mental functioning include loss of appetite (or preternaturally acute hunger), difficulty fixing attention, wandering thoughts, failing memory, enfeebled reasoning, prejudice replacing judgment, and possible subsequent physical nerve or brain disturbance leading to sudden collapse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These symptoms indicate that the reserve has been tapped and recuperative faculties arrested; they should be used to identify when worry, not mere fatigue, is producing dangerous disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and cultivate a reserve of mental energy; heed natural warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: A reserve of mental energy (stock in abeyance and base of every present act) is indispensable; pain, hunger, anxiety, and a sense of mind-weariness are warning tokens of exhaustion extending to the reserves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not override these signals; the reserve gives stability and 'rhythm' to mental action. Protect reserves by avoiding conditions that suspend warning senses (e.g., stimulants, overpowering impulses), and by ensuring appropriate rest/nutrition and habits that sustain tonicity of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention by education and correct training in brain-work
rubrics_metrics.description: Many instances of breakdown (sudden collapse) arise from lack of education in brain-work; untrained minds attempt feats for which training is indispensable. The utilitarian policy substituting results for processes and knowledge for education increases risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preventive measures include reversing policies that emphasize mere results, restoring processes that develop mental inelasticity, enforcing sedulous industry in youth, and providing proper training so minds are prepared for sustained intellectual work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Therapeutic principle: orderly, persistent work (not idleness) as cure
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind-cure for the malady to which 'worry' gives rise is not idleness or ordinary rest, but orderly and persistent work. The palsied faculties must be strengthened and incited to healthy nutrition by new activity, at first perhaps passive mental movement, then induced by appropriate stimuli applied to the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When worry has produced injury, gradually reintroduce structured mental activity to rebuild reserve and tonicity; avoid recommending idleness as a remedy and be wary of 'rest' as mere inactivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical standard for claims about national climate/character
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims comparing English and American climate and character must be borne out by careful study of facts on the ground (observation), not by exceptional or widely false generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extensive observation (e.g., study of crowds, comparison of villages, attention to varied social strata) and avoid relying on exceptional examples. The author emphasizes correcting popular ideas by direct study and comparison.
